name: Lacrosse
tagline: North America's oldest game — stick, ball, and a medicine returning to the Olympics in 2028.
overview: Lacrosse is played with a small solid rubber ball caught, carried, and thrown in the pocket of a long-handled stick called a crosse. Men's field lacrosse is 10 v 10 on a surface longer than a soccer pitch, women's field is 12 v 12 with finesse checking, and box lacrosse packs 6 v 6 into hockey rinks. A new 6 v 6 discipline called sixes was built by World Lacrosse specifically for the Olympic stage.

The game is the medicine game of the Haudenosaunee — tewaaraton, played for centuries as ritual, healing, and preparation for war — and the Haudenosaunee Nationals still compete among the world's elite as one of the few national teams defined by Indigenous identity. Lacrosse was an Olympic medal sport in 1904 and 1908, faded to demonstration status, and returns at the Los Angeles 2028 Games, a homecoming more than a century in the making.

Newcomers should know that stick skills are the whole sport. Catching and throwing with both hands inside the pocket decides everything else, and the fastest way to acquire them is daily wall work, not games. Learn to cradle before you learn to shoot.
facts: Tewaaraton, the Haudenosaunee medicine game — played long before European contact
1636 — French missionary Jean de Brébeuf names the game lacrosse after a bishop's crosier
World Lacrosse, formed in 2008 from the men's and women's federations and renamed in 2019 — more than 90 member nations
10 v 10 in men's field, 12 v 12 in the women's game, 6 v 6 in box lacrosse and sixes
Four quarters, 15 minutes each in NCAA play, with a shot clock in college and professional games
Field lacrosse pitch about 100.6 m by 54.9 m (110 by 60 yards); goals 1.8 m square
Medal sport in 1904 and 1908, demonstration until 1948, back on the program for Los Angeles 2028 in sixes
history: Pre-1500s
Haudenosaunee nations play tewaaraton as a healing ritual and warrior training — the medicine game of origin stories and community obligation.
Jesuit missionary Jean de Brébeuf records the game near the Georgian Bay and gives it the French name lacrosse.
Montreal Lacrosse Club forms in 1856; George Beers publishes uniform rules in 1867 and the National Lacrosse Association of Canada is founded.
Lacrosse is an Olympic medal sport at St. Louis and London; Canada wins both tournaments.
The International Lacrosse Federation forms in 1974; box lacrosse goes professional with the National Lacrosse League's first season in 1987.
The IOC grants provisional recognition in 2018, full recognition in 2021, and in 2023 confirms lacrosse's return at LA 2028 in the sixes format.
formats: Field lacrosse (men)
10 v 10 with body checking, long-stick defenders, and the six-across-midfield offside rule; NCAA games run four 15-minute quarters.
Field lacrosse (women)
12 v 12 with controlled stick checks only, stricter shooting-space rules, and a center draw to restart play.
Box lacrosse
6 v 6 inside hockey rinks with boards, a 30-second shot clock, and goalies who face a hail of close-range shots — the NLL's game.
Sixes
World Lacrosse's compact 6 v 6 format with four 8-minute quarters, no long poles, and a smaller field — built for the Olympics and emerging nations.
College lacrosse
The NCAA championships, for men since 1971 and women since 1982, remain the sport's biggest annual stage in the United States.
skills: Cradling
Rocking the stick with wrist and forearm so the ball stays seated in the pocket while running at speed.
Wall-ball with one hand on the shaft — 50 reps each side, then cradle through cones at full speed.
Catching and passing
Soft hands away from the body, then an overhand throw driven by the top hand pulling and the bottom hand pushing.
Partner lines at 10 and 20 meters; 100 clean catches before any shooting, half with the weak hand only.
Ground balls
Scooping through the ball with low hips and two hands — the scrappy skill that decides possession.
Roll the ball, scoop, sprint five steps; then make it a live 50-50 race against a partner.
Dodging
Split, roll, and bully dodges that beat a defender's stick and force the defense to slide.
1 v 1 alley runs to the cage with a live defender; the goal is to beat the stick, not the body.
Shooting
An overhand rip with torque from hips and shoulders, sidearm and underhand for changing angles and tight windows.
Static form first, then on-the-run shots from 5 and 10 meters, targeting the four corners of the 1.8 m goal.
Checking
Poke and slap checks with the stick to dislodge the ball; body contact is legal but tightly policed.
Poke-check repetition against a cradling partner — footwork first, stick second, head of the stick to the hands.
Face-offs and draws
The clamp, rake, and jam that restart play after every goal in the men's game; the draw does the same in the women's.
Whistle-to-whistle reps against a live opponent, tracking wins out of every 20 tries.
rules: Men's field lacrosse is 10 v 10; a team may not send more than six players across midfield on offense and must keep seven, usually including the goalie, back on defense.
Body checking is legal only against the ball-carrier or a player within five yards of a loose ball; hits to the head and from behind draw penalties.
The pocket must be legal depth — a stuck ball is raked free by the referee, and a pocket that traps too deep is a stick violation.
Penalties send players to the box for 30 seconds for technical fouls or one to three minutes for personal fouls, handing the opponent a man-up power play.
The women's game polices contact strictly: only controlled stick checks are legal, and a shooting-space violation protects players in front of the goal.
After every goal, men's play restarts with a face-off at center and women's play with a center draw.
College and professional games run a shot clock — 80 seconds in NCAA men's play — that forces a shot on goal or a turnover.
equipment: Head, pocket, and shaft; roughly 1.0-1.2 m for attackers and midfielders, with defensive long poles up to 1.8 m. A starter stick costs $60-150.
Solid vulcanized rubber weighing about 142 g; a dozen practice balls run $30-50.
Mandatory in men's field and all box play; $120-300.
Padded gloves, shoulder, rib, and arm protection in the men's game; a full set runs $100-250.
Protective goggles, mouthguard, and lighter gloves — simpler and cheaper at $50-120 for the set.
1.8 m square with netting; portable practice goals cost $150-400.
training: Stick skills are volume work: 15-20 minutes of daily wall-ball, alternating hands, does more than any gadget.
Lacrosse is change-of-direction sprinting — train deceleration and re-acceleration with lateral bounds and 5-10-5 shuttles.
Build a contact-ready core and neck; loaded carries and anti-rotation work transfer directly to legal checks and screens.
Goalies live on reps: 100 short-range reaction saves from a coach's flip per session, with the eyes leading the hands.
Condition for repeated 15-30 second sprints with incomplete rest — the exact rhythm of a shift, a ride, or a clear.
pathway: First stick
Parks programs and school clinics teach wall-ball and ground-ball games — the two skills everything else stands on.
Club and school
Town travel teams and high school lacrosse, where most American and Canadian players develop.
Showcase and college
Summer club circuits and recruiting camps feed NCAA rosters, the sport's de facto professional ladder.
Pro leagues
The Premier Lacrosse League for field and the National Lacrosse League for box pay the top players in the world.
International
World Championships every four years and the Haudenosaunee Nationals' seat among the elite set the global stage toward LA 2028.
events: Men's field world title, quadrennial since 1967; the United States leads with 11 championships to Canada's three.
The women's world championship, held since 1982, with the United States the dominant force and Australia its chief rival.
Box lacrosse's world title, staged since 2003 — Canada has won every edition.
The American professional field league, touring cities across a summer season since its 2019 launch.
Lacrosse returns as a medal sport in Los Angeles, contested in sixes for men and women.
legends: Jim Brown
A National Lacrosse Hall of Fame inductee and Syracuse All-American before his NFL fame — many still call him the greatest all-around athlete the sport has seen.
Gary Gait
Syracuse and Team Canada great whose vertical dunking redefined offensive lacrosse across a Hall of Fame field and box career.
Paul Gait
Gary's twin and partner — together the brothers rewrote what the stick could do, behind-the-back shots included.
Lyle Thompson
Haudenosaunee attacking great and two-time Tewaaraton Award winner (2014 and 2015) who plays the game the way it was invented — as a medicine.
Paul Rabil
Two-time NCAA champion at Johns Hopkins and co-founder of the Premier Lacrosse League; the sport's first modern entrepreneur-athlete.
getting_started: Buy a starter stick for $60-150 and find a wall; skip the padding until you know you are hooked.
Wall-ball every day — 20 minutes, 50 reps per hand — because catching and throwing are 90 percent of the sport.
Learn to cradle with both hands before you learn to shoot; weak-hand skill separates players faster than anything else.
Join a beginner league within a month; most cities run programs that lend sticks and teach the rules on the field.
Watch one Premier Lacrosse League weekend — the broadcast teaches field positioning better than any textbook.
If you come from hockey or basketball, try box lacrosse; the six-a-side game shortens the learning curve.
glossary: The full name of the stick — head, pocket, and shaft — from the French for a bishop's crosier.
Rocking the stick to keep the ball seated in the pocket while running or absorbing checks.
A loose ball on the turf; winning them decides games at every level.
A face-off move that pins the ball under the head of the stick to steal the first touch.
Moving the ball from defense to offense; failing to clear is a costly turnover.
Attacking the clear to trap the ball deep in the clearing team's end.
The double-team sent at the ball-carrier; sliding well is the heart of team defense.
The 2.74-meter circle around the goal that only the goalie and defenders may occupy.
The Mohawk name for the original game, little brother of war — also the college game's Heisman-style award.
The power play created when an opponent sits in the penalty box.

name: Volleyball
tagline: Six players, three touches, a net, and rallies that end two meters above the floor.
overview: Volleyball is two teams of six trading a ball over a 2.43-meter net for men and 2.24 meters for women on an 18-by-9-meter court. Each side may touch the ball three times — receive, set, attack — before sending it back, and every rally scores a point under the rally-scoring rules adopted worldwide in the late 1990s. Best-of-five sets to 25 points, with a deciding set to 15, make comebacks structural rather than lucky.

Invented as a gentler alternative to basketball for businessmen, it became one of the planet's most-played sports: the FIVB counts more than 220 member federations, and the Olympic tournament sits among the most-watched events of every Games. The sport's genius is scalability — the same rules govern a birthday-party court and the Volleyball Nations League final.

Newcomers should know that volleyball is won in the first touch. Serve-receive passing decides far more points than hitting, so the platform — joined forearms angled to target — is the first skill to own. Footwork for the approach comes before arm swings.
facts: 1895 — William G. Morgan, a YMCA director in Holyoke, Massachusetts, blends tennis, baseball, and basketball into a game first called Mintonette
FIVB, founded in Paris in 1947; over 220 national federations across five continental confederations
6 v 6 on court with rosters of 12 to 14; the libero defensive specialist entered the rules in 1998
Best of five sets to 25 points, fifth set to 15, all by two clear points — about 90-110 minutes
18 m by 9 m court with a 3-meter attack line; net at 2.43 m for men and 2.24 m for women
65-67 cm circumference and 260-280 g — bigger and lighter than a soccer ball
Medal sport for men and women since Tokyo 1964
history: William G. Morgan creates Mintonette at the Holyoke YMCA; a Springfield College professor renames it volleyball after watching the ball volleyed in flight.
The game travels through the YMCA network to Canada and Asia, and players in the Philippines develop the set and spike that turn volleyball athletic.
Fourteen federations found the FIVB in Paris; the first men's World Championship follows in Prague in 1949.
Volleyball debuts at the Tokyo Olympics; the Soviet Union takes the first men's gold and Japan the first women's.
The FIVB introduces rally scoring and the libero, ending the serve-and-sideout era and making every rally a point.
The Volleyball Nations League replaces the World League and Grand Prix as the sport's annual global circuit.
formats: Indoor 6 v 6
The Olympic game — three touches, rotations, libero, and the deepest tactical systems in the sport.
Beach volleyball
Two-a-side on sand, Olympic since 1996 and a fully separate discipline with its own page of this library.
Sitting volleyball
Paralympic sport for men since 1980 and women since 2004, played on a 10-by-6-meter court with a lower net and a fast ground game.
Nine-man volleyball
The nine-a-side Chinese-American tradition with no rotation and an open net game, anchored by the North American Chinese Invitational Volleyball Tournament since 1944.
Snow volleyball
A three-a-side winter variant recognized by the FIVB and played in boots and jackets on mountain snow.
skills: Serving
Float serves wobble without spin; jump serves are struck with topspin at over 100 km/h to break the first touch.
Serve 50 balls per session to three zones — deep corner, short middle, and the seam between passers.
Forearm passing
Platform contact with locked elbows and angled wrists; the ball rebounds off the platform rather than being caught.
100 passes against a partner's tosses, angled each rep into a marked target zone.
Setting
Fingertip contact in a window above the forehead with both hands finishing toward the target.
Self-toss, then 100 sets to a target circle; half of them back sets behind the head.
Attacking
A four-step approach, two-foot jump, and full arm swing with wrist snap on contact — power is timing, not muscle.
50 dry approaches without a ball, then hitting through controlled tosses with the block's hands as the target.
Blocking
Read the setter, seal the net with the hands, and penetrate over the tape into the hitter's airspace.
Mirror-jump drills against a setter, calling line or angle on every rep.
Digging
Defense below the tape — platform or overhead — with hips low and eyes on the hitter's arm swing.
A coach hitting from a box; dig 50 balls to a playable spot near the 3-meter line, not merely up.
Serve receive
The first touch that decides everything; passers form a triangle behind the 3-meter line.
Track your pass quality out of 50 serves received, aiming for 40 that reach the target.
rules: Six players a side; each team may touch the ball up to three times, and a block does not count as a touch.
Players rotate clockwise one position each time their team wins serve back, so every player attacks, sets, and defends in turn.
Rally scoring to 25 points in the first four sets and 15 in the fifth, always by a two-point margin, best of five sets.
The libero wears a contrasting color, cannot serve, block, or attack a ball above net height, and substitutes freely in back-row defensive spots.
Back-row players may not attack from above the top of the net or block in front of the 3-meter line.
Touching the net between the antennas, four team touches, or a caught-and-thrown ball hands the rally to the opponent.
Each team gets two 30-second timeouts per set.
equipment: FIVB-spec indoor ball of 65-67 cm and 260-280 g; a quality match ball runs $40-80.
The sport's signature protection for floor defense; $15-40.
Volleyball-specific court shoes with gum rubber soles and cushioned midsoles built for jumping; $70-150.
Adjustable poles and a net spanning about 9.5-10 m for an 18-by-9-meter court; home systems cost $150-400.
Red-and-white antennas mark the crossing plane above the net; all court lines are 5 cm wide.
Numbered jerseys with a contrasting libero kit, mandatory in organized play.
training: Count your jumps — spike, block, and serve loads tax knees and shoulders, so cap volume and land on two feet through the toes.
Train the vertical with loaded squats, trap-bar jumps, and low-volume high-quality plyometrics two or three times weekly.
Protect shoulders with external-rotation work and scapular control; rotator-cuff prehab is non-negotiable for attackers.
Rally fitness is repeat-sprint work: 15-30 second bursts with short rests mirror match demands better than long steady runs.
Serve-receive is trained, not hoped for — every session includes passing under pressure with consequences.
pathway: Backyard and school
The sport starts at picnics and gym classes; a ball and a rope net are enough to learn the three-touch rhythm.
Club volleyball
Regional clubs run tryouts, weekend tournaments, and positional coaching from roughly age 12.
National junior system
Provincial and junior national championships where national-team scouts do most of their watching.
Professional leagues
Italy, Poland, Japan, and Turkey run the strongest paid circuits, alongside growing leagues in Brazil, Iran, and China.
National team
The Olympic cycle and the Volleyball Nations League define the international calendar for the top 18 or so nations.
events: Every four years since 1964, twelve teams per gender after a worldwide qualification road.
The sport's oldest title, for men since 1949 and women since 1952, expanded to 32 teams on a two-year cycle from 2025.
The FIVB's annual traveling league since 2018 for the world's top national teams, built for broadcast.
The FIVB's annual club crown, long dominated by Brazilian and Italian powerhouses.
The European, Asian, Pan-American, and African titles each summer feed world qualification.
legends: Karch Kiraly
The only player with Olympic gold indoors in 1984 and 1988 and on the sand in 1996 — widely called the greatest volleyball player ever.
Regla Torres
Centerpiece of Cuba's three straight women's Olympic titles from 1992 to 2000, a gold medalist at 17 in Barcelona.
Giba
Brazil's attacking talisman of the 2000s — Olympic gold in 2004 and back-to-back world championships in 2002 and 2006.
Misty May-Treanor
Three Olympic beach golds from 2004 to 2012 alongside Kerri Walsh Jennings, after an NCAA indoor title with Long Beach State.
Kerri Walsh Jennings
The other half of beach volleyball's greatest dynasty — three golds, a 2016 bronze, and the longest winning streak the sport has known.
getting_started: Find a rec league or drop-in night; organized volleyball welcomes beginners far better than pickup parks.
Learn platform passing first — 15 minutes against a wall each day, then a partner.
Buy knee pads and court shoes before a fancy ball; your knees outlast your enthusiasm without them.
Practice the approach footwork off-ball until it is automatic; the arm swing is easy once the feet are right.
Watch NCAA finals or Volleyball Nations League rallies and count how many points are won on the first touch.
Play grass doubles or co-ed sixes weekly — more touches per person is the whole curriculum.
glossary: A serve that lands untouched or shatters the first pass.
An attack that ends the rally with a point, unbeatable by the defense.
A defensive recovery of a hard-driven attack.
A back-row attack launched from central court behind the 3-meter line.
Deliberately playing the ball off the blocker's hands and out for a point.
Two opposing players contesting the ball at the net tape at the same moment.
The setter's surprise second-touch attack over the net.
A wild first touch that flies nowhere near the setter.
Surrounding your own attacker to dig out a blocked ball.
The classic term for regaining serve — now slang for winning the rally off a strong defense.

name: Beach Volleyball
tagline: Two players, a mountain of sand, and every skill from block to swing owned by both.
overview: Beach volleyball is volleyball distilled: two players per side on a 16-by-8-meter sand court, playing best-of-three sets to 21 with a deciding set to 15. There are no substitutions and no coaching between points — whatever skill your pair lacks, one of you must provide it. The block counts as the team's first touch, so defense and attack flow through the same two athletes.

Born on the beaches of Santa Monica and raised in Manhattan Beach lore, the sport turned professional in the 1970s, joined the Olympics in 1996, and now sells out beaches on every continent. Every jump costs more in sand, every seam in the defense is man-made, and the communication between partners is the sport's hidden spectacle.

Newcomers should know that sand changes the game's physics: run to the ball and stop, set the ball clean and still, and read the wind before you read the opponent. Passing and setting under breeze are the first skills to train.
facts: 1920s — the sand courts of Santa Monica and Playa del Rey turned six-man volleyball into a beach phenomenon; the two-person game appears around 1930
FIVB runs the international game; the AVP has run the American professional tour since 1983
2 v 2 with no substitutions — block, dig, set, and attack from the same two people
Best of three sets, 21 points for the first two and 15 in the decider, always by two
16 m by 8 m court with at least 40 cm of sand; net heights identical to indoor at 2.43 m and 2.24 m
66-68 cm circumference, softer and lower-pressured than the indoor ball for control in wind
Olympic sport for men and women since Atlanta 1996
history: Beach volleyball grows out of Santa Monica's volleyball clubs; the first two-person game is played around 1930.
The first prize tournaments appear at Manhattan Beach, with winners reportedly collecting a crate of Pepsi-Cola.
The first open professional event draws the game's best to Will Rogers State Beach and beach volleyball becomes a career.
The Association of Volleyball Professionals forms to run the American tour.
The FIVB launches the international circuit with an event in Ipanema in 1987, beach volleyball debuts at the Atlanta Olympics in 1996, and the first World Championship follows in Los Angeles in 1997.
Misty May-Treanor and Kerri Walsh Jennings win three straight Olympic titles and 21 consecutive Olympic matches.
formats: Beach Pro Tour
The FIVB's international circuit since 2022, tiered from Futures through Challenge to Elite16 majors.
AVP tour
The American circuit since 1983 — the sport's spiritual home with its deepest professional fields.
World Championships
The FIVB's world title for national pairs, contested every two years since 1997.
NCAA beach volleyball
A fully sponsored American college sport since 2016 whose championship each May has built the women's talent pipeline.
Grassroots doubles
King and queen of the beach, co-ed quads, and park doubles — the formats every player starts in.
skills: Passing in sand
Run to the ball, then stop; the platform stays shallow because the sand absorbs the ball's pace.
A partner serves 50 balls from the far side; land each pass inside a 2-meter circle near the net.
Beach setting
Clean, still hands — spinning or drifting overhand sets are whistled, and setting over the net with fingers is illegal.
Set 100 balls in a cross-breeze, chasing stillness at the moment of contact.
Attacking into space
With only one blocker, every swing has a seam; cut shots and high hands over the block replace raw power.
Split the court with cones and hit 30 balls to each seam at match speed.
Blocking and pulling
Call line or angle for your partner, block, then pull off the net on defense to dig behind your own hands.
Block-pull-dig repetitions with a coach calling shots; the communication is part of the rep.
Jousting
The contested ball at the tape, won with patience and strong wrists rather than brute strength.
Partner jousts on a call — hold the high hands and finish the push upward and over.
Serving in wind
Shortened-toss jump floats into the wind, heavy topspin with the wind at your back.
Serve 30 balls per session alternating wind directions, tracking aces and broken passes.
Sand movement
Shorter, quicker steps with an upright posture; takeoffs sink, so jumping is trained differently from indoor.
Sand sprints of 4 by 20 meters with walk-back rests, plus low box jumps on firm ground.
rules: Two players per side, no substitutions and no coaching between points — the pair solves everything itself.
The court is 16 by 8 meters with the same net heights as indoor; elite sand must be at least 40 cm deep.
Rally scoring to 21 for the first two sets and 15 in the third, by two clear points, with sides switching every 7 points played (every 5 in the decider).
An overhand set must be clean and still — spin or drift is a fault — and finger sets over the net are illegal.
The block counts as the first of the team's touches, leaving two contacts to dig and set or set and attack.
A hard-driven ball may be received with an overhand double-contact beach dig only as the first team touch.
Partners alternate serves, and either player may attack from anywhere on their side of the net.
equipment: Fine, drained sand at least 40 cm deep at the elite level; any deep-sand beach or park court works to learn.
A softer, larger-feeling ball of 66-68 cm with lower air pressure; $30-60.
Polarized, strap-secured glasses are standard professional kit against glare and kicked sand; $50-200.
Neoprene socks against burning courts — the one purchase that saves more beginner sessions than any other; $15-40.
Ribbon or taped boundaries strung at the corners; portable line sets cost $50-100.
A net and poles set outside the 8-meter court; portable systems run $200-500.
training: Sand makes you strong: sprints, bounds, and jump repetitions in soft sand build legs that transfer to every surface.
Jump mechanics change on sand — train shorter, faster ground contact and count jumps to manage load in summer heat.
Shoulder and core endurance for high swing volume; band work and rotational medicine-ball throws are the standard.
Train heat tolerance and hydration deliberately — elite matches run 90 minutes in midday sun with no shade.
Play mixed doubles and king-of-the-beach formats; touching every role accelerates the judgment that two-a-side demands.
pathway: Park doubles
A net, four players, and a summer evening — the entry point for nearly everyone.
Local club circuit
Regional tournaments teach the two-person game's tactics, switching systems, and unwritten etiquette.
National junior tour
Youth and junior championships in the United States, Brazil, and Europe feed the professional pipeline.
Pro circuit
Futures and Challenge events lead to Elite16 majors and, in time, the two-year Olympic qualification race.
Olympic Games
Quota places are earned through world rankings over the cycle — the sport's summit every four years.
events: Every four years since 1996, 24 pairs per gender qualifying through a two-year rankings race.
The world title for national pairs, every two years since 1997.
The top tier of the annual FIVB circuit since 2022, featuring the world's leading 16 pairs.
The American tour's summer run from Huntington Beach to Chicago, with the AVP Championships closing the year.
American college beach volleyball's team title, contested each May since 2016.
legends: Karch Kiraly
The only player with indoor golds in 1984 and 1988 and a beach gold in 1996 with Kent Steffes — the bridge between the two games.
Misty May-Treanor
Three Olympic titles from 2004 to 2012 and 21 straight Olympic match wins — the winningest competitor the sport has seen.
Kerri Walsh Jennings
May-Treanor's partner across the dynasty, an Olympic bronze in 2016 with April Ross at 37, and the sport's great ambassador.
Emanuel Rego
Brazil's tactical master — Olympic champion in Athens 2004 with Ricardo Santos after a record-setting world-title career.
Phil Dalhausser
The Thin Beast — 2008 Olympic champion and one of the game's great blocking and net-defense artists.
getting_started: Find sand: most large cities maintain beach courts, and an hour of play costs nothing but sunscreen.
Learn the two-touch rhythm early — the block counts as your first touch, so dig and set become one motion.
Serve a float first; power serves are wasted in wind until the toss is consistent.
Play with many partners — the sport's real vocabulary is communication, and it is learned by talking.
Buy sand socks before summer courts burn your feet; burned feet end more beginner careers than bad passes.
Watch an AVP final for the block-pull system, then replay one point and name every call made.
glossary: The blocker dropping off the net to play defense after the serve — a signature beach move.
A sharp-angled attack sliced with topspin into the open corner.
A contested ball at the tape, won by whoever pushes last and strongest.
A one-handed defensive dig played with the knuckles.
An overhead, spread-finger dig used to absorb a hard-driven first ball — legal on the first team touch only.
A one-armed block, the other hand kept out of play — a beach improvisation.
The gap between two defenders, or between blocker and digger, that attacks are aimed into.
Winning the rally on defense to regain the serve — the term that once named the old scoring system.
Reading the breeze — floaters served into the wind, heavy topspin served with it.
The defensive position pulled well off the net behind the block.

name: Handball (Team Handball)
tagline: Basketball's footwork with soccer's goals and a full-speed collision in between.
overview: Team handball is 7 v 7 on a 40-by-20-meter court, two 30-minute halves, and a ball thrown at 3-by-2-meter goals guarded by keepers who fill most of them. Players dribble, take three steps, hold the ball three seconds, and launch themselves from outside the 6-meter line to shoot over or through defenses. Scores of 25 to 30 goals a side are normal, and a goal arrives roughly every 40 seconds.

It is Europe's second indoor religion — enormous in Germany, the Nordic countries, France, Spain, the Balkans, and North Africa — and its Champions League Final4 in Cologne sells out 20,000 seats like a cup final. The French call their golden generation Les Experts; the Danes turned the last decade into a dynasty.

Newcomers should know that the footwork rules are the game's grammar: three steps, then dribble or pass, with the jump shot learned from a standstill before ever moving. The goalkeeper is a spectacle in their own right and the sport's most specialized craft.
facts: 1917 — modern rules published in Germany, drawing on Danish haandbold traditions of the 1890s
International Handball Federation (IHF), founded 1946 in Copenhagen; more than 200 member federations
7 v 7 on court — six field players and a goalkeeper — with unlimited flying substitutions
Two 30-minute halves with a running clock; drawn knockout matches add two 5-minute overtime periods
40 m by 20 m court with 3-by-2-meter goals and a 6-meter goal-area line
58-60 cm and 425-475 g for men; 54-56 cm and 325-375 g for women
Indoor handball Olympic since Munich 1972 for men and Montreal 1976 for women; the outdoor 11-a-side game appeared in 1936
history: Danish gym teachers and German school reformers such as Holger Nielsen and Konrad Koch codify the ball games that converge into handball; the first modern rules appear in Berlin in 1917.
The International Amateur Handball Federation forms in 1928; outdoor 11-a-side handball is an Olympic sport at the 1936 Berlin Games.
Germany hosts and wins the first indoor seven-a-side World Championship, born as a winter alternative to the field game.
Eight nations found the IHF in Copenhagen, and indoor play steadily replaces the outdoor field game worldwide.
Indoor handball debuts at the Munich Olympics; the women's tournament follows in Montreal in 1976.
France's Les Experts win six world titles and three Olympic golds; Denmark then answers with three straight men's world championships from 2021 to 2025.
formats: Indoor 7 v 7
The Olympic standard: 40-by-20-meter court, two 30-minute halves, and the world's strongest leagues in Europe.
Beach handball
4 v 4 on sand with spin shots and keeper goals worth two points — an IHF world title since 2016 and a Youth Olympic Games sport in 2014.
Field handball
The original 11-a-side outdoor game, Olympic in 1936 and still played in Germany and Scandinavia as a heritage format.
Mini handball
Smaller courts, lighter balls, and simplified rules for children under eight — the entry point across European schools.
skills: Jump shot
The signature throw — drive, leap, and release at the apex over defenders or the keeper's shoulder.
60 shots per session from three angles: center, back position, and 9 meters.
Wing play
Corner attackers who score from impossible angles, often airborne outside the court when they release.
50 flying shots per session, turning in the air past a coach-thrown keeper cue.
Pivot play
The line player who screens, seals, and finishes from 6 meters among the defense.
Footwork ladders, then catch-and-finish repetitions with a passive defender to beat.
Passing
Overhead, bounce, behind-the-back, and spin passes — all one-handed, many from the air.
Pair passing in continuous motion for 10 minutes without feet ever stopping.
6-0 defense
The flat six-man wall with step-out pressure — handball's most common defensive shape.
Shadow drills where defenders shift as one unit on a coach's point calls.
Goalkeeping
Close-range shot-stopping with split-second reads; keepers are the sport's celebrities.
Massed-shot blocks of 100 throws, reacting to hip, arm, and foot fakes.
Fast break
Goalkeeper save to sprinting wing in under five seconds — the game's most electric sequence.
Break drills: keeper outlet to two runners against one defender, ten repetitions each direction.
rules: Seven players a side with unlimited rolling substitutions — the game never stops for changes.
Field players may take three steps, hold the ball three seconds, and dribble freely; dribbling resets the step count.
Only the goalkeeper may stand inside the 6-meter goal area; attackers may leap into it if they release the ball before landing.
A clear scoring chance illegally stopped gives a 7-meter penalty throw; lesser fouls give a 9-meter free throw from the dashed line.
Defenders may use their torso to block but must not hold, hit, or push; rough play brings two-minute suspensions, and a third sends the player off.
Each team gets three 60-second team timeouts per match.
The clock stops in the last minute of each half and for team timeouts, keeping late finishes live.
equipment: Resin-friendly leather or synthetic balls — 58-60 cm for men, 54-56 cm for women; $40-90.
3-by-2-meter frames with nets; club-grade goals cost $500-1,500, so beginners play in gyms with supplied ones.
Indoor court shoes with strong lateral support for cutting; $60-130.
Sticky rosin that improves grip on leather balls — standard at elite level, banned in some youth leagues; $10-20.
Long trousers, padded sleeves, and knee protection; $80-200.
Numbered jerseys with contrasting goalkeeper colors, mandatory in organized play.
training: Handball is repeat-sprint anaerobic work — train 10-30 meter accelerations with short recoveries, the rhythm of each attack.
Jump power for the shot: countermovement jumps, single-leg bounds, and landing mechanics that spare knees and ankles.
Shoulders take the beating — manage throw volume and commit to rotator-cuff and scapular work to prevent the sport's overuse injuries.
Footwork rules mean agility ladders and 1-2-3 step patterns practiced until they are reflex.
Goalkeepers train like wrestlers: hip mobility, video-based reaction work, and massed shot-blocking.
pathway: School and mini handball
Small balls and small courts from age six across European school systems.
Club youth
Academies at clubs such as Kiel, Barcelona, and Veszprém scout early and train three to four times weekly.
National junior teams
Under-18 and Under-20 world and European tournaments mark the elite track.
Professional leagues
Germany's Handball-Bundesliga and the EHF Champions League sit at the peak of club play.
National team
World Championships now biennial and Olympics every four years define the international calendar.
events: For men since 1938 and women since 1957 — France leads the men's roll with six titles, Denmark the reigning force.
Every Games since Munich 1972, twelve teams per gender.
Europe's club crown, decided since 2010 at the Final4 weekend in Cologne.
The continental title for men and women, biennial since 1994.
The sand game's world title, staged since 2016.
legends: Nikola Karabatić
France's midfield general — a triple Olympic champion and four-time world champion, the greatest two-way player of his era.
Mikkel Hansen
Denmark's left back — Olympic champion in Rio 2016 and world champion in 2021 and 2023, the most feared shooter of his generation.
Thierry Omeyer
The goalkeeper of France's golden generation — two Olympic golds and multiple world titles behind the Les Experts wall.
Ivano Balić
Croatia's Olympic champion of 2004 and world champion of 2003 — the most watchable playmaker of the 2000s.
Cristina Neagu
Romania's left back, a four-time IHF World Player of the Year and a Champions League great with Győr.
getting_started: Join a club or university team — the footwork rules need live defenders to make sense.
Learn the three-step rhythm first: catch, two steps, jump — the entire game lives in this footwork.
Master the standing jump shot before running; 30 shots per session builds arm-safe mechanics.
Play 4 v 4 on a half court to multiply touches; the 40-meter court divides beautifully into drills.
Watch the EHF Champions League Final4 — the broadcast teaches court geometry and defensive shifts.
Start shoulder prehab on day one; the throwing load is high and the injuries are preventable.
glossary: The free throw taken from the dashed line for ordinary fouls.
The penalty shot from 7 meters for a clear chance illegally denied.
The goal-area boundary only the goalkeeper may stand inside.
The line player operating among the defenders at the 6-meter line.
The corner attacker, usually the smallest and quickest player on the court.
A jump shot where the throwing arm circles over the head to disguise the angle.
The counterattack launched straight from a keeper save or turnover.
The referee's raised-hand warning when a team stops attacking; possession is forfeited if it continues.
Defenders guarding areas rather than players — the default 6-0 wall.
A two-minute exclusion for fouls, during which the team plays a player short.

name: Netball
tagline: Basketball's Commonwealth cousin — seven positions, three seconds, and sniper shooting.
overview: Netball is 7 v 7 with fixed positions — goalkeeper, goal defense, wing defense, center, wing attack, goal attack, goal shooter — each confined to designated thirds of a 30.5-by-15.25-meter court. Only the two shooters may score through a 3.05-meter ring with no backboard, no player may run with the ball, and the holder must pass within three seconds. Defenders must stand 0.9 meters away before contesting a pass.

It is one of the world's most-played women's team sports, with about 20 million players across more than 80 nations, and its culture is shaped by women's leadership from club committees to the international federation. Australia and New Zealand have traded supremacy for a century, with England's 2018 Commonwealth gold the great heist of the modern era.

Newcomers should know that the footwork rule is the whole education: land, pivot on the landing foot, and pass inside three seconds. Shooting without a backboard rewards repetition like almost nothing else in sport.
facts: 1890s — an adapted, outdoor women's version of basketball spread from English colleges across the British Empire
World Netball — the international federation founded in 1960 and renamed from IFNA in 2020
7 v 7 with fixed positions and squads of 12 using rolling substitutions
Four 15-minute quarters, 60 minutes total, with tactical and injury stoppages
30.5 m by 15.25 m court split into thirds; goal post 3.05 m tall with a 38 cm ring
690-710 mm circumference and 400-450 g — leather or composite
Not on the Olympic program; a Commonwealth Games core sport since 1998 and IOC-recognized since 1995
history: Basketball arrives at a Hampstead physical-training college and mutates for outdoor play; American Clara Baer publishes her related basquette rules in 1895, and the first codified net ball rules appear in England in 1901.
The All England Netball Association forms and standardizes the rules the Empire plays.
England, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and the West Indies found the international federation; the first World Tournament follows in 1963 at Eastbourne.
The IOC grants the federation full recognition — a milestone for a women-run international federation.
Netball debuts at the Commonwealth Games in Kuala Lumpur, where Australia and New Zealand's final runs to double overtime.
Australia and New Zealand launch new professional leagues; England stun Australia with a last-second goal for Commonwealth gold in 2018.
formats: Traditional 7s
The world game — fixed positions, court thirds, and 60-minute internationals.
Fast5
Five-a-side with four 6-minute quarters, power plays, and 2- and 3-point super shots from range — the made-for-television version.
Mixed and social netball
The recreational lifeblood of Australia, New Zealand, and Britain, with indoor centers running leagues nightly.
Walking netball
A slower variant championed by England Netball for over-50s and returning players.
Indoor netball
A netted-court version with rebound walls, popular in South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand.
skills: Shooting
The goal shooter and goal attack score from inside the 4.9-meter-radius circle with a one-hand guided release and repeatable rhythm.
Shoot 100 reps per session from five spots in the circle and track makes out of 100.
Footwork
Land, pivot on the landing foot, and pass within three seconds — the game's defining constraint.
Shuttle pivots: catch, land, pivot 180 degrees, pass — 50 reps each side.
Passing variety
Chest, shoulder, bounce, overhead, and lobbed circle entries, chosen by the defense in front of you.
Triangle passing with a defender in the middle for 10 minutes of continuous work.
Defensive marking
Mark the player and the space, then deny the pass lane with an active leading hand.
One-on-one mirroring: 30-second holds where the attacker may not receive.
Interception
Reading angles and leaping the lane for a turnover — the game's most valuable single act.
Two lines pass across a defender who times the jump; chase 20 interceptions per session.
Center-court control
The center links defense to attack through all three thirds within the three-second rule.
Conditioning runs stitched with decision drills — pass within two seconds of every catch.
Circle defense and rebounding
Goal defense and goalkeeper contest the shot and win the rebound off a rim with no backboard.
30 shots with defenders required to win the loose ball 20 times.
rules: Seven fixed positions — GK, GD, WD, C, WA, GA, GS — each restricted to defined thirds, and only the two shooters may score.
No running or dribbling with the ball; the holder must pass within three seconds of catching.
The first landing foot is the pivot foot; dragging or re-planting it is footwork and gives the ball to the opponents.
Defenders must be 0.9 meters from the passer's landing feet before actively defending the pass — closer is obstruction.
Contact and obstruction award a penalty pass with the offender standing out of play; minor infringements give a free pass.
Entering a forbidden third, even for a loose ball, is offside.
Four 15-minute quarters with rolling substitutions; finals use extra time for drawn matches.
equipment: 3.05 m posts with a 38 cm steel ring and no backboard — accuracy is absolute.
Position-lettered bibs from GK to GS, color-coded per team; $15-30.
Lateral-support court shoes with grip for hard outdoor and indoor courts; $60-120.
30.5 by 15.25 meters with thirds, center circle, and goal circles marked on a hard surface.
A whistle and a current rulebook — umpiring is a recognized and respected career track in the sport.
training: Netball is repeated accelerations and lateral movement: shuttle runs and 5-0-5 agility tests mirror match demands.
Single-leg strength and balance matter because pivoting and landing dominate — split squats and Copenhagen planks are staples.
Vertical power for rebounds and interceptions through low-volume plyometrics twice a week.
Ankle and knee injury prevention is central — netball's landing injuries rank among the highest in women's sport, so landing mechanics are coached explicitly.
Elite shooters take 200-plus practice shots daily; the ring forgives nothing and rewards nothing else.
pathway: School and junior netball
Almost every girl in Australia, New Zealand, and much of the Commonwealth starts in school netball.
Club and representative
Regional leagues and age-group representative teams from about age 12 upward.
Semi-professional leagues
Australia's Suncorp Super Netball, New Zealand's ANZ Premiership, and England's Netball Super League pay the top tier.
National selection
National squads and the Commonwealth Games and World Cup cycle define the elite calendar.
Officiating and coaching
The sport's women-led governance makes umpiring and coaching genuine career ladders.
events: Every four years since 1963 — Australia leads with a dozen titles, Trinidad and Tobago's 1987 upset the great outlier.
A core sport since 1998; England's 2018 gold ended the Australian-New Zealand duopoly.
Australia's eight-team professional league since 2017 and the world's richest.
The annual Australia-New Zealand test series, the sport's fiercest rivalry.
legends: Irene van Dyk
New Zealand's goal shoot and the most-capped player in international netball history with more than 200 tests for South Africa and then New Zealand.
Liz Ellis
Australia's long-serving captain, a two-time world champion and Commonwealth gold medalist, now the sport's leading broadcaster and advocate.
Vicki Wilson
Australia's sharpshooting goal attack of the 1990s and later a championship-winning coach in the ANZ era.
Helen Housby
England's shooter whose last-second goal won the 2018 Commonwealth gold — the most famous shot in the sport's history.
Casey Kopua
New Zealand's inspirational defensive captain and a 2019 world champion after returning from retirement.
getting_started: Find a local association — in Australia and New Zealand a club sits within minutes of nearly every suburb.
Learn the positions by playing every one; the rules only make sense from inside each third.
Practice pivots daily: catch, land, hold three seconds, pass — footwork faults are the beginner's whole education.
Shoot 50 balls after every session; the ring has no backboard to forgive you.
Watch a Suncorp Super Netball match to see the 0.9-meter defense and circle feeds in action.
Umpire a junior game — it is the fastest way to learn the rules and the sport values it highly.
glossary: GK, GD, WD, C, WA, GA, GS — the seven fixed roles; only the two shooters can score.
The rule against re-planting or dragging the landing foot while holding the ball.
Defending closer than 0.9 meters to the player with the ball.
Any illegal interference with an opponent, from pushing to leaning on a landing player.
Restart awarded for minor infringements, taken from the spot.
Awarded for contact or obstruction, taken with the offender standing out of play.
Coordinated movement between shooters and feeders inside the goal circle.
The pass into the shooting circle to the shooters.
The alternating restart taken by the center after every goal.
A defender tipping the ball without catching it to create a turnover.

name: Gaelic Football
tagline: Ireland's amateur giant — soccer's skills, rugby's collisions, and aerial ballet on top.
overview: Gaelic football is 15 v 15 on a pitch larger than soccer's, played with a round ball that may be kicked, fisted, and caught but never thrown. One point goes over the H-shaped crossbar, three under it for a goal, and since 2025 scores struck from beyond a 40-meter arc count two. Players carry the ball by soloing — bouncing and toe-tapping it off the boot — and tackles are shoulder charges and ball-slaps only.

The game is the showpiece of the Gaelic Athletic Association, founded in 1884 to revive Irish games, and it stays proudly amateur at every level: county stars hold day jobs and return each week to their parish clubs. The All-Ireland final fills Croke Park's 82,300 seats — among the largest crowds in European sport — for players who are paid in pride.

Newcomers should know the core rhythm is catch, solo, pass, with kicking demanded of every position and both feet. The mark, the shoulder, and the 40-meter arc are the three rules that most change how the modern game looks.
facts: 1884 — the Gaelic Athletic Association forms in Thurles to revive Ireland's native games
The GAA, with thousands of clubs at home and abroad; the Ladies Gaelic Football Association has run the women's game since 1974
15 v 15 with limited substitutions from a panel
70 minutes at senior inter-county level, 60 minutes below it
130-145 m long by 70-82 m wide, with H-shaped posts and a goal mouth 6.4 m wide and 2.44 m high
1 point over the bar, 3 for a goal under it, 2 for scores from beyond the 40-meter arc since 2025
Never Olympic — the All-Ireland final and the intermittent International Rules series with Australia are its world stage
history: Folk football has been played in Ireland for centuries — the Statutes of Kilkenny tried to ban it in 1366, proof of its grip.
Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin found the GAA in Thurles; the first All-Ireland championships are played in 1887.
The Sam Maguire Cup is presented to the All-Ireland football champions.
The Ladies Gaelic Football Association is founded — now one of the world's largest women's sports organizations.
Dublin win six consecutive All-Irelands, the modern standard of dominance.
The Football Review Committee introduces sweeping changes, led by two-point scores from beyond the 40-meter arc.
formats: Inter-county championship
The pinnacle: provincial titles feed the All-Ireland series each summer, ending at Croke Park in July.
National Football League
The divisional league each spring — promotion, relegation, and the form lines for the championship.
Club football
The soul of the GAA: parish teams whose county finals are the most fervent occasions in Irish sport, where the county stars return.
Ladies football
15-a-side under the LGFA with closely aligned rules and its own All-Ireland final for the Brendan Martin Cup.
International Rules
Hybrid Tests against Australia's AFL professionals blending both codes' rules, played intermittently since 1984.
skills: Solo
Dropping the ball onto the boot every few strides — one bounce, then toe-taps — lets a player run legally at full speed.
Solo relays: 30 meters down and back, alternating feet, ten lengths without losing the ball.
Catching and fielding
High catches and palmed grabs above opponents' heads — the game's signature aerial contest.
20 high balls per session, kicked by a partner from distance, caught above a static opponent.
Hand pass
A struck pass off the fist — throwing is illegal — and the game's metronome for possession.
Fist-pass rondos in a tight grid, 50 passes each hand, eyes up.
Kick passing
The drop kick with the laces, long and short, off both feet — the sport's defining skill.
Kick-pass grids where every second pass must travel more than 20 meters and swap feet.
Shooting
Points from 40-plus meters off the drop kick, and placed goals under the bar from angles.
Score 50 attempts from the arc, then 30 placed shots at goal from close range.
Tackling
Legal contact is the shoulder charge and the slap at the ball — never the grab.
Live 1 v 1 grids with a referee enforcing shoulder-only contact.
Kickout play
Goalkeepers restart after scores and wides; the long kickout became the game's strategic battleground.
Keeper target drills: 20 kickouts per session to marked zones with pressure arriving.
rules: Fifteen players a side; the ball may be kicked, fisted, and caught but never thrown.
Run with the ball by alternating bounces and toe-taps — the ball cannot be bounced twice in a row.
Scoring: one point over the crossbar, three under it, and since 2025 two points from beyond the 40-meter arc.
Tackling is by shoulder charge and ball-slap only; grabbing the jersey or body gives away a free.
The ball cannot be picked directly off the ground with the hands — lift it with the foot or scoop it on the run.
A clean catch from a kick that traveled over 20 meters can be called as a mark, rewarding the catcher with a free.
Goalkeepers restart with kickouts after scores and wides; senior inter-county halves run 35 minutes with stoppages built in.
equipment: Size 5, 480-500 g, leather-look panels built for both hands and boots; $25-80.
Club jersey, shorts, and socks — the colors carry civic and parish identity.
Grip gloves are common and optional; $15-40.
130-145 by 70-82 meters with H-posts, shared with hurling across the GAA calendar.
training: Players cover 8-12 kilometers per match with repeated high-speed segments — build the aerobic base and add speed endurance and change of direction.
Aerial strength for catching under contact: trap-bar deadlifts, hip power, and core anti-rotation work.
Ball skills are volume: kick-passing ladders and solo drills woven into every run.
Shoulder-proofing for legal contact — neck and upper-back work reduces the sting of big hits.
County players juggle day jobs with professional-level training loads, so sleep and load management are treated as skills.
pathway: Schools and nurseries
GAA club nurseries take children from age five; almost every parish runs one.
Under-age county
Development squads and the minor championship, plus schools' and universities' competitions like the Hogan and Sigerson Cups.
Senior club
The local championship is where reputations are made and county managers watch.
Inter-county panel
Amateur in name only — professional training, nutrition, and analysis around the day job.
Management
The coaching ladder runs from club sideline to county management and All-Ireland glory.
events: The summer championship culminating at Croke Park — the biggest day in Irish sport.
Divisional league each spring, with promotion, relegation, and form lines for the championship.
Munster, Leinster, Connacht, and Ulster titles — Ulster's famously the toughest.
The LGFA championship for the Brendan Martin Cup, with Meath's back-to-back titles in 2021 and 2022 recent lore.
Ireland versus Australia in hybrid rules, intermittent since 1984 — a nod to the games' shared family tree.
legends: Colm Cooper
Kerry's Gooch — five All-Irelands and the forward whose swagger defined the 2000s.
David Clifford
Kerry's generational forward and All-Ireland winner in 2022 and 2025.
Stephen Cluxton
Dublin's revolutionary goalkeeper whose long kickouts changed the sport — eight All-Ireland medals across a two-decade career.
Cora Staunton
Mayo's four-time All-Ireland winner and one of ladies football's first superstars, later an AFLW professional with Greater Western Sydney.
Peter Canavan
Tyrone's all-time great forward, driving the county to its first All-Ireland in 2003.
getting_started: Find a GAA club — every parish in Ireland has one, and most cities abroad have a county's club.
Learn solo and fist-pass in week one; they are the alphabet of the game.
Kick with both feet from the start — weak-side kicking is the fastest differentiator.
Play lots of 1 v 1 with shoulder contact to learn what is legal early.
Watch an All-Ireland final archive — Kerry-Dublin classics show the aerial game at its best.
Expect the club to be the center of the experience; the GAA is a community institution first and a league second.
glossary: The run-carry: dropping the ball to the boot every few strides.
A struck pass off the fist — throwing is illegal.
A clean catch from a long kick, rewarded with a free.
The goalkeeper's restart after a score or a wide.
A free from the touchline after the ball goes out of play.
An attacker inside the small square before the ball arrives — the score is disallowed.
Using the hands to deflect a kick as it is struck.
The legal body tackle — big hits are part of the game.
A free from the 45-meter line awarded when a defender is last to touch the ball over their own end line.
The local community the club represents — the GAA's basic unit.

name: Hurling
tagline: Three thousand years old, 150 km/h off the stick — Ireland's ancient game of air and nerve.
overview: Hurling is 15 v 15 with a flat ash stick — the camán, or hurley — and a small hard leather ball, the sliotar, struck over a crossbar for one point and under it for a three-point goal. The ball flies at up to 150 km/h, is caught cleanly in the hand, balanced on the bas, pulled off the ground, and contested in the air at full sprint. It is routinely called the world's fastest field sport.

The game runs through Irish myth — the boy Setanta tames the hound of Culann with a sliotar and becomes Cú Chulainn — and through 3,000 years of recorded history, surviving bans and famine to be codified by the GAA in 1884. Like its sibling Gaelic football, it remains amateur at every level, played before 82,000 at the All-Ireland final by men and women with day jobs.

Newcomers should know that hurling rewards nerve and symmetry: striking off both sides of the bas, catching under rain and pressure, and playing the ball off the turf with a stick while everyone else sprints at you. The wall is the first gym.
facts: For at least 3,000 years — one of the world's oldest field games, present in Irish myth and early law tracts
1884 — the GAA writes uniform rules at its founding in Thurles
The GAA for hurling; the Camogie Association, founded in 1904, runs the women's game
15 v 15, the same as Gaelic football, on the same pitch
1 point over the crossbar, 3 for a goal; the sliotar is 69-72 mm across and 110-116 g
Not Olympic — the All-Ireland final and the club game are its world stage
history: Myth and law
Hurling fills Irish mythology — Setanta's feat makes him Cú Chulainn — and early Irish law tracts regulate the game's violence.
The Statutes of Kilkenny try to ban English colonists from playing hurling — evidence of how thoroughly the game thrived.
The GAA codifies hurling at its founding in Thurles; the first All-Ireland championship is played in 1887.
The Camogie Association forms to run the women's game, with nearly identical rules.
Limerick lift the first Liam MacCarthy Cup as senior champions.
Limerick win five titles in six years, including four in a row from 2020 to 2023.
formats: Inter-county hurling
The pinnacle: provincial and All-Ireland championships each summer, ending at Croke Park.
Club hurling
The parish game — the grassroots backbone, with county club finals that stop towns.
Camogie
The women's game since 1904, with its own All-Ireland final for the O'Duffy Cup and near-identical rules.
Hurling-shinty internationals
Composite-rules Tests against Scotland's shinty players, a nod to the games' shared ancestry.
Sevens and urban hurling
Seven-a-side festival tournaments and school programs that keep the game growing in cities.
skills: Striking
From the hand and off the ground, off both sides of the bas — accuracy at speed decides everything.
Wall striking: 100 shots per side, then moving targets at 20 and 45 meters.
Catching
Bare-hand high catches with soft hands and the free hand guarding the body.
High-ball contests: 20 balls pucked high by a partner over a static opponent.
Blocking
Standing in front of an opponent's swing with the hurley held square — courage with technique.
Block repetitions against a live striker starting from five meters.
Hooking
Flicking your bas over the opponent's from behind as the swing begins — timing is everything.
30 successful hooks per drill block in 1 v 1 striking games.
The pull
The low, forceful ground stroke that sends the sliotar 80-plus meters.
Ground-pull reps along a line, then pulling out of defense under pressure.
Sideline cut
The celebrated strike off the turf from a sideline ball — accuracy's hardest test.
50 sideline attempts per session, alternating sides of the bas.
Puck-out
The goalkeeper's restart after every wide or score — modern keepers pick targets like quarterbacks.
20 targeted puck-outs per session to marked receivers with pressure arriving.
rules: Fifteen players a side on the Gaelic pitch; over the crossbar scores one point, under it scores three.
The sliotar may be caught in the hand, but on the ground it may only be played with the hurley or the foot — never picked up by hand.
Tackling means the shoulder, the block, and the hook; swinging at the player rather than the ball is a foul.
The ball may be carried in the hand or balanced and tossed on the bas while running — the solo run.
Every wide or score ends with the goalkeeper's puck-out; sideline balls are struck off the turf.
A foul denying a goal gives a penalty from the 20-meter line — one striker against the keeper.
Senior matches run 70 minutes, and the All-Ireland final fills Croke Park's 82,300 seats for an amateur game.
equipment: A flat-ended ash stick cut to suit the player, with a maximum blade width of 13 cm; $40-120.
Leather over a cork core, 69-72 mm across and 110-116 g — hard-cored and fast off the bas; $15-30.
Mandatory with faceguard at all levels since 2010; $60-150.
Optional fingerless gloves improve grip and protect the knuckles; $20-40.
Players keep a spare on the line — breakages are part of every match.
training: Striking volume is everything: 15 minutes of daily wall-ball, both sides, is the hurler's daily bread.
Rotation power comes from hips and trunk — medicine-ball rotational throws and cable pulls build the pull.
Hands and reaction: catching drills with varied pucks, juggling, and reaction-ball work for a ball moving at 150 km/h.
Deceleration and change of direction on grass, with Nordic curls and Copenhagen planks for a sprint-heavy game.
Aerial courage is trained: paired high-ball drills with a designated catcher build the confidence the game demands.
pathway: Club nursery
GAA Cúl Camps and school programs introduce the camán to thousands each summer.
Under-age club and school
Under-age leagues and schools cups; the best play minor county at 17.
Adult club
County championships — the club is where careers are measured.
Inter-county
Panels train like professionals while remaining amateur, five nights a week around jobs and study.
Coaching
Games promotion officers and coaching ladders sustain the game's growth at the grassroots.
events: The summer championship ending in the Liam MacCarthy final before a full Croke Park.
Munster's round-robin is the game's crucible — Cork, Tipperary, Limerick, Clare, and Waterford in one gauntlet.
The women's championship, run since 1932 for the O'Duffy Cup.
The spring league under lights, a form-builder for the championship.
Ireland versus Scotland each year in composite rules, honoring the games' shared ancestry.
legends: Christy Ring
Cork's sorcerer of the 1940s and 1950s — eight All-Irelands and the standard by which all hurlers are measured.
Henry Shefflin
Kilkenny's ten-time All-Ireland winner and three-time Hurler of the Year — the modern benchmark.
DJ Carey
Kilkenny's darling of the 1990s and 2000s, a multiple All-Ireland winner and Hurler of the Year whose fame crossed county lines.
Joe Canning
Galway's long-range artist, finally lifting Liam MacCarthy in 2017 as Hurler of the Year.
Nickey Rackard
Wexford's 1950s icon, remembered in the name of the Nicky Rackard Cup.
getting_started: Buy a cheap hurley and sliotar and find a wall — hurling's first gym is a gable end.
Strike 100 balls off both sides of the bas every session; symmetry decides who plays.
Learn the jab lift — scooping the ball off the ground with the hurley — 50 reps per session.
Play wall games with a partner; live catching under pressure is learned only live.
Watch a Munster round-robin match — the noise alone teaches the stakes.
Join a club adult beginner group; most GAA clubs now run them and lend gear.
glossary: The hurley — the flat ash stick every player carries.
The ball: cork core, leather cover, and 110-116 g of menace.
The flat striking end of the hurley.
The goalkeeper's restart after a wide or a score.
The spectacular ground strike from a sideline ball.
The low power stroke along the ground.
Tossing the sliotar on the bas while running.
Scooping the ball off the ground with the hurley while moving.
A tackle from behind that checks the opponent's swing mid-motion.
A flicked pass with the hand — struck, not thrown.

name: Australian Rules Football (AFL)
tagline: Eighteen a side, no offside, and the greatest jumping catch in world sport.
overview: Australian football is 18 v 18 on cricket ovals up to 185 meters long, with no offside and all 36 players sharing one oval ball. Kicking is the primary skill, handballing is a fist pass off the palm, and a clean catch from a 15-meter kick is a mark — a free kick, taken or played on. Goals between the two inner posts score six, behinds score one, and four 20-minute quarters with time-on make matches about two and a half hours of real time.

It is Australia's winter religion: the most-attended sports league in the country, a Grand Final before about 100,000 at the MCG, and a code invented in Melbourne in 1858 to keep cricketers fit that became a national identity. The women's AFLW, launched in 2017, now matches the men's 18 clubs.

Newcomers should know three things define the game: the mark, the drop punt, and the fact that no position is offside. Learn to kick end-over-end accurately and catch everything, and the rest is running.
facts: 1858-1859 — Tom Wills calls for a football club to keep cricketers fit, and Melbourne FC writes the first ten rules in May 1859
The Australian Football League — the VFL, founded 1897, renamed AFL in 1990 — with state leagues and AFLW beneath it
18 a side on the field with a free-running interchange bench
Four 20-minute quarters plus time-on — about two and a half hours of real time
Ovals 135-185 m long and 110-155 m wide — the largest playing surfaces in world football
6 points between the inner posts, 1 for the outer behind posts; 80-110 points a side is a normal scoreline
Not Olympic; the AFL International Cup is the global stage for developing football nations
history: Tom Wills and friends stage the first matches in Melbourne; the Melbourne Football Club codifies the first rules in May 1859.
The Victorian Football Association forms in 1877; the VFL breaks away with eight clubs in 1897 and becomes the competition that matters.
The Brownlow Medal, for the season's fairest and best player, is first presented.
South Melbourne relocates to Sydney in 1982, the league nationalizes across Australia, and the VFL is renamed the AFL in 1990.
The first AFL International Cup draws national teams of amateur players from around the world.
AFLW launches with eight clubs — professional women's football begins, expanding to 18 clubs within six seasons.
formats: AFL
The national league: 18 clubs playing a 23-round home-and-away season into a four-week finals series.
AFLW
The women's league since 2017, now matching the men's 18 clubs, running from August to a late-November final.
State leagues
The SANFL, WAFL, and VFL — historic competitions that develop talent and hold the game's depth.
AFL 9s
The official small-sided format: nine a side with modified contact, built for social and workplace leagues.
International Cup
Staged in Australia roughly every three to four years for national teams from countries where the game is growing.
skills: Kicking (drop punt)
The default kick — ball held point-down and struck end-over-end, accurate to a target 50 meters away.
Kick 50 balls to a partner at 20-50 meters; 8 of 10 should hit the chest at 30 meters.
Marking
Catching a kicked ball cleanly — chest marks, high marks, and the contested speccy overhead.
Contested marking grids of 3 v 1 with high kicks; 30 grabs per session.
Handball
Held on one palm and punched with the fist of the other — the game's quick-release pass.
Handball chains: 10-minute continuous grids where only fists move the ball.
Ground balls and tackling
Winning the contest at the feet and wrapping the ball-carrier legally between shoulders and knees.
Tackle-bag repetitions and four-player ground-ball races.
Shepherding
Using the body to shield a teammate or block a runner between kicks — legal where most sports call it obstruction.
2 v 2 protect-the-carrier drills with a coach policing the legal bump.
Rucking
The contested tap at every center bounce and boundary throw-in.
Jump-timing drills against a live opponent, tapping to marked zones set by a coach.
Set-shot kicking
Conversion from angles after a mark or free kick — pressure is mental and mechanical.
50 set shots from the arc with a 7-of-10 target from 40 meters.
rules: Eighteen a side with free interchange; there is no offside — all 36 players contest one ball on one oval.
A mark is a clean catch from a kick that traveled 15 meters or more; the marker takes the free or plays on immediately.
Scoring: 6 points between the two inner posts, 1 point for the outer behind posts or when the ball crosses the line off a defender.
A player running with the ball must bounce or touch it on the ground every 15 meters.
Tackles must wrap between the shoulders and knees; high contact and pushes in the back are free kicks.
Kicking the ball out of bounds on the full concedes a free kick from the boundary; other out-of-bounds plays restart with a throw-in.
Four 20-minute quarters with time-on added for stoppages; finals resolve draws with extra time.
equipment: The Sherrin — a leather-look oval ball about 72 cm around and 450-500 g; official match balls cost $100 and up, trainers $30-60.
Low-cut boots with molded studs for hard Australian ovals; $80-180.
The numbered club jumper, mandatory in organized play.
Two inner goal posts 6.4 m apart with behind posts 6.4 m further out either side, on ovals up to 185 m long.
The entire beginner kit — the game's beauty at entry level is its simplicity.
training: AFL players run 12-18 kilometers per match with repeated high-speed efforts — build the aerobic base, then add speed endurance.
Jumping and landing under contact on grass, with lower-body strength blocks periodized around the season.
Kicking is a skill of thousands of repetitions — sessions begin and end with goal-kicking ladders.
Contact conditioning and safe tackling technique, with neck and upper-body strength for contests.
Recovery is professional-grade even below the AFL: sleep, soft-tissue work, and load management across a long season.
pathway: Auskick
The national beginner program for ages 5-12 — fun-first and contact-light.
Community clubs
Local leagues from under-10s through seniors — the heartbeat of Australian country towns and suburbs.
State leagues and academies
SANFL, WAFL, and VFL competition plus AFL club talent academies feed the draft.
The draft and AFL
The national draft assigns teenage talent to clubs; careers are built on multi-year contracts.
AFLW and beyond
The women's pathway mirrors the men's, and coaching, umpiring, and media are full careers.
events: Late September at the MCG before about 100,000 — the biggest event on the Australian sporting calendar.
The fairest-and-best count, held on the Monday night before the Grand Final.
The women's league runs from August to a late-November grand final.
Amateur national teams from around the world, staged in Australia since 2002.
The SANFL and WAFL finals carry over a century of history each.
legends: Leigh Matthews
Lethal — a four-time premiership Hawk named the AFL player of the century in 2000, then a premiership coach.
Tony Lockett
The most prolific goal-kicker in VFL and AFL history with 1,360 career goals.
Lance Franklin
Buddy — 1,000-plus goals across Hawthorn and Sydney, the first to the milestone since Lockett and the most magnetic forward of the modern era.
Ron Barassi
Ten premierships across playing and coaching and the game's first celebrity tactician.
Daisy Pearce
The face of women's football before AFLW, captain of Melbourne's 2022 premiership, and now a leading broadcaster and assistant coach.
getting_started: Join Auskick or a social AFL 9s league — both are built for first-timers.
Learn the drop punt before any other kick; 20 minutes a day against a wall or with a partner.
Catch everything — the mark is the game's joy, and hands are trained by volume.
Watch one quarter of an AFL match following only one midfielder's running patterns.
Expect to run: build a 5-kilometer base before your first season.
Find a local club open day — Australian clubs recruit as much by community as by trial.
glossary: The spectacular high mark — the airborne catch taken above a pack of players.
Legally blocking an opponent with the body to protect a teammate or the ball.
The fist pass struck off the palm — the game's quick-release option.
A curved kick struck around the body, used from tight angles.
A rapidly executed kick over the shoulder toward goal in traffic.
The tall player contesting every center bounce and boundary throw-in.
The spiral-nosed punt for maximum distance.
The one-point score through the outer posts.
The bench rotation — players swap on the fly through the interchange gate.
The timekeeper's signal ending each quarter — play stops instantly.

name: Ultimate
tagline: Seven a side, no referees, and a Spirit of the Game that actually works.
overview: Ultimate is 7 v 7 on a 100-by-37-meter field with two 18-meter end zones, scored by catching a 175-gram disc in the opponent's end zone. The disc cannot be run with — the thrower must keep a pivot foot planted while a defender counts the stall to ten — and any incomplete pass is an immediate turnover. Games run to 15 points or a time cap, with no physical contact allowed.

What makes the sport singular is Spirit of the Game: matches are self-officiated even at world championships, with players calling their own fouls and resolving disputes on the field. The WFDF holds full IOC recognition, ultimate has been a World Games sport since 2001, and its mixed-gender divisions are standard rather than exceptions.

Newcomers should know that throwing is 80 percent of the game. The backhand and forehand grips, the wrist snap, and three simple cuts learned at full speed will make anyone playable within a month — the sport's communities are famously built to teach exactly that.
facts: 1968 — students at Columbia High School in Maplewood, New Jersey, with Joel Silver among the founders, adapt Frisbee football into a played sport
World Flying Disc Federation (WFDF, founded 1985); USA Ultimate governs the American game
7 v 7 outdoors, 5 v 5 on beach and indoor; mixed-gender rosters are standard at world level
Games to 15 points, or time-capped at roughly 90-100 minutes
100 m by 37 m including two 18-meter end zones — the length of a soccer pitch at about half its width
The standard 175-gram disc, 27.4 cm in diameter
Not yet Olympic; played at The World Games since 2001 with the WFDF fully IOC-recognized since 2015
history: Columbia High School students play the first games in the school parking lot, and the rules spread through New Jersey high schools.
Late 1970s
The Ultimate Players Association — now USA Ultimate — organizes the American game.
The first world championship is played in Gothenburg, Sweden.
The World Flying Disc Federation is founded to govern disc sports internationally.
Ultimate debuts at The World Games in Akita, Japan — its first multi-sport stage.
The IOC grants the WFDF provisional recognition in 2013 and full recognition in 2015.
formats: Outdoor 7s
The classic game on full grass fields, in open, women's, and mixed divisions.
Beach ultimate
5 v 5 on a 75-by-25-meter sand field — the sport's sunshine format with its own world championships.
Indoor ultimate
5 v 5 in sports halls, popular across northern Europe through the winter.
Professional leagues
The American Ultimate Disc League, running since 2012, plays with officials and a game clock.
College ultimate
USA Ultimate's college series is the talent engine; the Callahan Award honors its top graduating players.
skills: Backhand
The default throw — power from the hips, release flat from the chest, with the wrist snap doing the work.
100 throws to a partner at 10-30 meters before adding a defender's mark.
Forehand (flick)
The tight-window release with the middle finger on the rim and the thumb steadying the flight plate.
30 throws at 10, 20, and 30 meters each, focusing on a flat spin.
Huck
The long throw downfield of 50-70 meters with height and hang time for the receivers to run under.
Huck into a marked 10-meter circle from 50 meters, alternating both throws.
Cutting
The in-cut, deep cut, and dump cut — sudden changes at full speed that sell the fake and create separation.
Two-line cutting drills: plant hard on the go call and attack the disc's shoulder.
Layout
The full-extension dive for a catch or block — the sport's signature act.
Learn in slow motion on soft grass; 20 layouts per session once landing mechanics are safe.
Marking
The mark counts the stall and shapes the thrower's angles, removing half the field without touching the disc.
Hold a force for ten full stalls against a live thrower, arms wide, hips low.
Handler movement
Swings and reset passes that move the disc through the backfield while cutters clear space.
3-handler weave drills with a stall count running on every possession.
rules: Seven a side; the disc may be thrown anywhere but never run with — the pivot foot stays planted while holding it.
The thrower has ten seconds on the stall count; a completed count is a turnover.
An incomplete pass — dropped, intercepted, out of bounds, or hitting the ground — is an immediate turnover, and play continues.
Points are scored by catching the disc in the opponent's end zone; after each score, the scoring team throws off the pull.
Games are self-officiated under Spirit of the Game: players call their own fouls, and a contested call returns the disc to the thrower.
Substitutions happen only between points and for injuries.
Contact is a foul; dangerous plays and disc-space violations are called by the player affected.
equipment: The official 175-gram disc of 27.4 cm diameter; $10-20.
Molded cleats with ankle support for cutting on grass; $60-150.
Lightweight jerseys and shorts — most clubs design their own, and team culture is part of the sport.
Two dozen per field — ultimate's fields are lined with cones rather than paint.
Tournament days mean four to six matches in the sun, so water and shade planning is standard equipment.
training: The engine is repeated sprints — 30-60 meter cuts with short rests, trained with intervals that match point rhythms.
Change-of-direction strength: Nordic curls and Copenhagen planks prevent the hamstring and groin tears the sport produces.
Throwing is weather-proof volume — 15 minutes daily of flicks, backhands, and hucks, deliberately into wind.
